definition: Threat classification framework: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. Maps to six security properties (authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability, authorization).
Visual notation for threat modeling with five elements: external entities, processes, data stores, data flows, and trust boundaries. Trust boundaries are where threats live.
A boundary in a data flow diagram where trust level changes (e.g., user to server, public internet to VPC). Every STRIDE threat maps to a trust boundary crossing.
A one-way function that produces a fixed-size output from arbitrary input. Cannot be reversed. Used for password storage (bcrypt, Argon2) and integrity (SHA-256).
Reversible transformation of plaintext to ciphertext using a key. Provides confidentiality. Symmetric (AES) uses same key; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses public/private key pair.
Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode. Authenticated encryption (AEAD) — provides both confidentiality and integrity. Standard choice for encrypting data at rest and in transit.

Number used once. A random or sequential value that ensures the same plaintext encrypted with the same key produces different ciphertext. Reusing a nonce in AES-GCM is catastrophic — it leaks the XOR of two plaintexts.
A deliberately slow password hashing function with built-in salt and configurable work factor (cost). Designed to resist brute-force attacks. Never use SHA-256 or MD5 for passwords.
A random value added to each password before hashing. Ensures identical passwords produce different hashes, preventing rainbow table attacks.
Checking that data conforms to expected patterns before processing. Use allow-lists (define valid input) over block-lists (enumerate bad input). Validate at the trust boundary.
Transforming data so it can be safely inserted into a specific context (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, URL). Context-aware encoding prevents injection attacks. Use framework-provided encoders.
A validation strategy that defines what valid input looks like and rejects everything else. More robust than block-lists because it's future-proof against novel attacks.
Secure Software Development Lifecycle. Integrates security activities into every development phase: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, operations.
Moving security activities earlier in the development lifecycle. A vulnerability caught in design costs ~$10 to fix; the same vulnerability in production can cost $100,000+.
Static Application Security Testing. Scans source code for vulnerability patterns without running the application. Examples: Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube. Run in CI/CD on every push.
Dynamic Application Security Testing. Scans the running application by sending attack payloads. Examples: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Run against staging environments.
Insertion of malicious SQL into an application query via string concatenation. Allows attackers to read, modify, or delete database contents. Prevented by parameterized queries.

A query where the structure is fixed and user input is bound as parameters, never concatenated into SQL. The database treats parameter values as data, not code. The primary defense against SQL injection.

SQL injection where the application doesn't return query results directly. The attacker infers data from behavioral differences: boolean-based (true/false responses) or time-based (deliberate delays).
Cross-Site Scripting. Injection of malicious JavaScript into pages viewed by other users. Three types: reflected (in URL), stored (in database), DOM-based (client-side only).
Content Security Policy. A browser-enforced security header that controls which script sources are allowed. Prevents XSS exploitation when configured correctly (no unsafe-inline).
A client-side HTML sanitizer that removes dangerous elements and attributes from user-supplied HTML. Use when rich HTML rendering is unavoidable. Never write your own sanitizer.
Cross-Site Request Forgery. An attacker tricks a victim's browser into making an unwanted request to a site where they're authenticated. Prevented by anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
A cookie attribute (None, Lax, Strict) that controls when cookies are attached to cross-site requests. SameSite=Lax blocks CSRF on POST requests while preserving normal navigation.
A random token generated server-side, embedded in forms, and validated on state-changing requests. Attackers cannot read the token due to Same-Origin Policy. Primary CSRF defense.

Insecure Direct Object Reference. Accessing another user's data by changing an identifier in a request. Prevented by ownership checks — always verify the requester is authorized to access the resource.
Server-Side Request Forgery. Tricking a server into making requests to unintended locations, often cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254). Prevented by URL allow-lists and network segmentation.
HTTP Strict Transport Security. A response header that forces browsers to use HTTPS. Prevents SSL stripping and cookie hijacking. Format: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains.
JSON Web Token. A signed token with three segments: header, payload, signature. Used for stateless authentication. Payload is encoded (not encrypted) — never put secrets in claims.
Authorization framework for delegated access. A user grants a third-party app limited access without sharing credentials. Authorization Code + PKCE is the standard grant for public clients.

Proof Key for Code Exchange. A security extension for OAuth 2.0 that prevents authorization code interception. The client proves possession of a code_verifier that matches the code_challenge sent in the authorization request.

A query language for APIs where clients specify exactly what data they want. Introduces unique attack surfaces: introspection abuse, deep query DoS, batch attacks, and field-level authorization requirements.
Controlling the rate of requests to an API. Algorithms: token bucket (burst-tolerant), leaky bucket (constant rate), sliding window (no boundary effects). Prevents brute-force, scraping, and DoS.
A rate limiting algorithm where a bucket holds tokens that refill at a constant rate. Each request consumes a token. Allows bursts up to bucket capacity, then throttles to refill rate.
Managing changes to API contracts. Strategies: URL path (/v2/), header (Accept: version=2), query param (?version=2). Old versions must be sunset — deprecated endpoints leak data.
Verifying identity — "Are you who you claim to be?" Methods: passwords, MFA, WebAuthn, passkeys. Distinct from authorization (permissions).
Determining permissions — "Are you allowed to do this?" Models: RBAC (roles), ABAC (attributes), DAC (owner-controlled), MAC (policy-controlled). Applied on every request after authentication.
An attack where the attacker forces a victim to use a known session ID, then hijacks the authenticated session. Prevented by regenerating the session ID on login.
Multi-Factor Authentication. Requires two or more different factor types: something you know (password), have (TOTP, hardware key), or are (biometric). TOTP is preferred over SMS.
A cookie flag that prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie via document.cookie. Mitigates cookie theft via XSS. Session tokens should always be httpOnly.
Tricking a user into clicking something different from what they perceive by overlaying transparent iframes. Prevented by X-Frame-Options: DENY or CSP frame-ancestors.
The ten most critical web application security risks, published by OWASP. Updated periodically. 2021 edition: Broken Access Control (A01), Cryptographic Failures (A02), Injection (A03).
Common Vulnerability Scoring System. A numerical score (0-10) representing the severity of a vulnerability. Factors: attack vector, complexity, privileges required, user interaction, scope, impact.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. A unique identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability. Format: CVE-YYYY-NNNNN. Used by SCA tools to match dependencies against known vulnerabilities.
Software Bill of Materials. A machine-readable inventory of all components, libraries, and dependencies in a software product. Used for supply chain transparency and vulnerability management.
Software Composition Analysis. Scanning dependencies for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and license compliance issues. Tools: Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check.
A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor and has no patch available. Zero-day exploits are highly valuable and used in targeted attacks before disclosure.
Web Application Firewall. A network-layer defense that inspects HTTP traffic for attack patterns. A defense-in-depth layer — attackers can bypass WAFs. Never rely on a WAF as your only defense.
Automated testing that sends malformed or random input to software interfaces to discover crashes and unexpected behavior. Effective for parsers, file formats, and protocol implementations.

Manual security assessment by trained testers who attempt to exploit vulnerabilities. Finds business logic flaws that automated tools miss. Point-in-time assessment — not a substitute for continuous security.

Transport Layer Security. Cryptographic protocol for secure communication over networks. TLS 1.3 is current. Provides encryption, authentication, and integrity. Never design your own transport protocol.
Restricting which TLS certificates an application trusts to a specific set. Prevents MITM attacks via compromised CAs. Used in mobile apps for API communication.

Writing data past the end of an allocated buffer, overwriting adjacent memory. Can overwrite return addresses to hijack execution flow. Prevented by bounds checking, safe libraries, and stack canaries.
Address Space Layout Randomization. Randomizes the memory location of code, stack, and heap at load time. Makes buffer overflow exploitation harder — attacker cannot predict target addresses.
A random value placed on the stack before the return address. Checked before function return — if overwritten (buffer overflow), the program aborts. Named after canaries in coal mines.
No-eXecute / Data Execution Prevention. Marks memory regions as non-executable. Prevents shellcode execution on the stack or heap. Part of the W^X (write XOR execute) principle.

Time of Check to Time of Use. A race condition where a resource's state changes between when it's checked and when it's used. Example: checking file permissions, then opening the file — the file may have been replaced.
Identity and Access Management. Cloud-native access control. Define who (principal) can do what (action) on which resource, under what conditions. Principle of least privilege applies.

Every component should have the minimum permissions required to function. Database accounts, IAM roles, API keys — limit blast radius. If an attacker compromises a component, they get only its permissions.
Securing containerized applications: use minimal base images, run as non-root, drop capabilities, scan images for vulnerabilities, use read-only filesystems.
Role-Based Access Control in Kubernetes. Defines which users/service accounts can perform which operations on which resources within a namespace or cluster-wide.
Infrastructure as Code. Managing infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files (Terraform, CloudFormation). IaC scanning detects misconfigurations before deployment.
Secure storage and distribution of credentials, API keys, tokens, and certificates. Use a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). Never hardcode secrets in source code or config files.

Security Information and Event Management. Centralized log aggregation, correlation, and alerting. Ships security events (auth failures, privilege changes) to a central system for detection and response.

Documented process for handling security incidents: detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Tested via tabletop exercises. Defines roles, escalation, and notification procedures.

An attack where a malicious package is published with the same name as an internal private package. The package manager resolves to the public (attacker's) version. Prevented by scoped packages and registry configuration.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts. A framework for ensuring software artifact integrity from source to deployment. Levels 1-4 represent increasing provenance and build integrity guarantees.
Securing the continuous integration and delivery pipeline: protect secrets, validate dependencies, run SAST/SCA/secret scanning, sign artifacts, control who can trigger deployments.
A fast, open-source static analysis tool that finds vulnerability patterns in source code using pattern matching. Supports 30+ languages. Run in CI/CD and pre-commit hooks.
The standard web application security testing tool. Features: intercepting proxy, scanner, repeater, intruder, decoder. Used for manual and automated testing of web applications.
Automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool. Can detect injection points, enumerate databases, dump data, and obtain OS shells on the database server.

Remote Code Execution. The ability for an attacker to execute arbitrary code on a target system. The most severe vulnerability class. Can result from deserialization, injection, buffer overflows, or file upload flaws.

A browser security mechanism that restricts how documents and scripts from one origin can interact with resources from another origin. Prevents cross-site reading of data. The foundation of web security.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. A mechanism that relaxes the Same-Origin Policy for specific origins. Must be configured carefully — overly permissive CORS allows cross-site attacks.
A cryptographic hash function that is cryptographically broken. Collisions can be generated in seconds. Never use for security purposes. Use SHA-256 for hashing, bcrypt for passwords.
Electronic Codebook — an AES mode where each block is encrypted independently. Reveals data patterns in ciphertext. Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. Never use.
The winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015). Memory-hard password hashing function resistant to GPU and ASIC attacks. Successor to bcrypt. Use for new systems.
Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. A key exchange protocol that allows two parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel. Used in TLS 1.3 and Signal Protocol.
A modern elliptic curve designed for speed, security, and misuse resistance. Used in TLS 1.3, Signal, WireGuard, and SSH. Preferred over NIST P-256 for new systems.

An HTTP response header that controls whether a page can be embedded in an iframe. Values: DENY (never), SAMEORIGIN (same origin only). Prevents clickjacking. CSP frame-ancestors is the modern replacement.
An HTTP header that prevents MIME type sniffing. Value: nosniff. Without this, browsers may execute files as scripts even when served with a different Content-Type.
A DOM property that parses and renders HTML strings. Dangerous with untrusted data — any <script> tag executes. Use textContent for text; DOMPurify for sanitized HTML.
React's escape hatch for rendering raw HTML. The name is a warning. Must be paired with DOMPurify or equivalent sanitization when using untrusted data.
OpenID Connect. An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. Adds an id_token (JWT) containing user claims. OAuth for authorization, OIDC for authentication.
A long-lived OAuth token used to obtain new access tokens. Should be rotated on each use — old token invalidated. Stored securely (HttpOnly cookie, device keychain).
Distributed Denial of Service. Overwhelming a service with traffic from many sources. Rate limiting and CDN/WAF protection mitigate application-layer DDoS.
A URL that links to a specific screen or content within a mobile app. Can be hijacked if the app doesn't validate the link's parameters — leading to unauthorized actions.
Android Package Kit. The file format for Android applications. Can be decompiled and analyzed for hardcoded secrets, insecure configurations, and vulnerable libraries.

Detecting whether a mobile device has been jailbroken (iOS) or rooted (Android). Compromised devices bypass OS security controls. Apps may refuse to run or restrict functionality on compromised devices.
Infrastructure as Code tool by HashiCorp. Defines cloud resources declaratively. IaC scanning (Checkov, tfsec) detects misconfigurations before apply.
Instructions for building a Docker container image. Security: use minimal base images, run as non-root USER, use COPY instead of ADD, don't expose unnecessary ports.
Digitally signing software to verify its origin and integrity. Users can verify the software hasn't been tampered with since the developer signed it. Part of the SLSA framework.
Registering package names that are common misspellings of popular packages (e.g., requets instead of requests). Users who mistype install the attacker's package.

A browser API that prevents DOM-based XSS by requiring dangerous sinks (innerHTML, document.write) to accept TrustedHTML objects, not raw strings. Enforced via CSP: require-trusted-types-for 'script'.

When both vulnerabilities exist on the same site, XSS bypasses CSRF protections. Injected JS can read anti-CSRF tokens from the DOM, read cookies, and forge authenticated requests with custom headers.
Google's CAPTCHA service that distinguishes humans from bots. Used to prevent automated account creation, credential stuffing, and scraping. Can be bypassed by determined attackers.
Automated login attempts using username/password pairs from breached databases. Relies on password reuse across sites. Mitigated by MFA, rate limiting, and breached password detection.
See SSRF. An attack where the server is tricked into making requests to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints on behalf of the attacker.
An attack that changes a domain's DNS record between when the hostname is validated (points to public IP) and when the request is made (points to internal IP). Bypasses SSRF hostname allow-lists.
GraphQL operation types: queries read data, mutations write data. Both can be vulnerable to injection, excessive data exposure, and authorization bypass if not properly secured.
Pre-registered GraphQL queries identified by hash. Only allowed queries execute — blocks introspection abuse and restricts the attack surface. Used by Apollo and Relay.
Representational State Transfer. An architectural style for APIs using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources identified by URLs. Stateless — each request is independent.
Web Authentication API. A browser standard for passwordless authentication using hardware security keys or platform authenticators (fingerprint, face). Phishing-resistant — tied to the origin.
FIDO2-based credential that replaces passwords. Synced across devices via platform keychain (iCloud, Google Password Manager). Phishing-resistant and cryptographically strong.
A password-based key derivation function designed to be memory-hard. Like bcrypt but also requires significant memory, making GPU/ASIC attacks more expensive.
Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2. Applies a hash function many times (iterations) to derive a key from a password. Weaker than bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 but still used in legacy systems.
Software that generates, stores, and autofills strong unique passwords per site. Eliminates password reuse and weak passwords. The single most effective security tool for end users.
An immutable record of security-relevant events: logins, privilege changes, data access, configuration changes. Used for detection, forensics, and compliance. Must be tamper-proof.

A program where organizations reward external researchers for responsibly disclosing vulnerabilities. Provides a legal safe harbor for good-faith research. Managed via platforms like HackerOne or Bugcrowd.
Information about current and emerging threats: attacker TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, Procedures), IOCs (Indicators of Compromise), and vulnerability exploitation trends.

A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Used for threat modeling, detection engineering, and red teaming. Organized by tactic (goal) and technique (method).
Code or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability to cause unintended behavior: code execution, privilege escalation, data exfiltration, denial of service.
The part of an attack that performs the malicious action: the SQL injection string, the XSS script, the reverse shell command. Distinct from the delivery mechanism (the request, the link).
A connection initiated from the target machine back to the attacker, giving the attacker command-line access. Often the goal of RCE exploitation.
An isolated environment for running untrusted code. Browser sandboxes isolate tabs; Docker containers isolate processes; VM sandboxes isolate operating systems.
A decoy system designed to attract attackers and study their behavior. Can detect intrusions, gather threat intelligence, and waste attacker resources.
Security Operations Center. A team responsible for monitoring, detecting, and responding to security incidents 24/7. Uses SIEM, SOAR, and threat intelligence platforms.
Denial of Service. Making a service unavailable to legitimate users by exhausting resources: CPU, memory, network bandwidth, or application threads.
A flaw where the system's behavior depends on the timing of events. In security contexts: TOCTOU (file checks), double-spend (financial transactions), concurrent session manipulation.
Dynamically allocated memory managed by the application. Heap-based vulnerabilities: use-after-free (accessing freed memory), double-free (freeing twice), heap overflow (writing past allocation).
Accessing memory after it has been freed. The freed memory may be reallocated to another object — the attacker controls what the dangling pointer references.
A vulnerability where user input is used as the format string in printf-style functions. Attackers can read stack memory or write to arbitrary addresses using %n.

The memory region allocated on the call stack for a single function invocation, containing local variables, the saved frame pointer, and the return address. Stack overflows overwrite adjacent frames toward higher addresses.
The instruction pointer value saved on the stack when a function is called, so execution can resume after the function returns. The primary target of stack buffer overflow attacks.

Exploit technique chaining short existing instruction sequences (gadgets) each ending in RET to achieve arbitrary computation without injecting new code. Bypasses NX/DEP by reusing code already in memory.
A short sequence of existing instructions ending in RET, used as a building block in ROP chains. Attackers string gadgets together to perform arbitrary computation from existing code.
Stack overflow technique overwriting the return address to call a libc function (e.g., system("/bin/sh")) rather than injecting shellcode. Bypasses NX because it jumps to existing executable code.
Position-independent machine code injected into a process and executed by an attacker, typically spawning a shell. Requires NX to be absent or bypassed.

A binary compiled to load at a random base address (via -fPIE -pie), enabling ASLR for the executable's own code and data segments. Without PIE, the binary's own addresses are fixed even with ASLR on.
Relocation Read-Only. A linker mitigation (-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now) that marks the GOT read-only after all symbols are resolved, preventing GOT overwrite attacks from format string bugs or heap exploits.

A data table in ELF binaries storing resolved addresses of dynamically linked functions. Writing a function pointer here (via format string or heap exploit) redirects all calls to that function. Full RELRO makes it read-only.
Trampoline stubs in ELF binaries that implement lazy symbol resolution on first call. Each PLT entry jumps through the corresponding GOT slot. Overwriting GOT redirects PLT calls.

Mitigation restricting indirect calls and returns to only valid targets defined at compile time. Forward-edge CFI (Clang CFI, Intel IBT) validates call targets; backward-edge CFI (shadow stack) validates return addresses.

A hardware-protected copy of return addresses (Intel CET) maintained in memory inaccessible to normal writes. On function return, the CPU compares the stack return address against the shadow stack value.

Executable and Linkable Format. The binary format used on Linux for executables, shared libraries (.so), and relocatable object files (.o). Contains code, data, symbol tables, and sections like .text, .data, .got, .plt.

Per-thread free chunk cache in glibc malloc (2.26+). Freed same-size chunks are returned to a singly-linked per-thread list and reused LIFO. Minimal integrity checks make tcache poisoning (overwriting the next pointer) a common heap exploit primitive.
A pointer to memory that has been freed but not set to NULL. Dereferencing it reads or writes whatever has been allocated in that slot since — the foundation of use-after-free exploits.
Freeing the same heap chunk twice. Corrupts the allocator's free list metadata, often allowing the chunk to appear twice in the free list and be allocated to two different callers simultaneously.

Attack embedding shellcode or ROP gadgets inside JIT-compiled executable pages by crafting script with large immediate constants that appear verbatim in the emitted machine code. Bypasses NX without writing to executable pages directly.
JIT compiler mitigation XORing all large immediate constants with a per-session random key before emitting code. The in-memory bytes are unpredictable, preventing JIT spraying gadget placement.

CPU microarchitecture attack (CVE-2017-5753/5715) exploiting speculative execution and branch prediction to transiently access out-of-bounds memory, encoding the value in the CPU cache as a side channel.

CPU microarchitecture attack (CVE-2017-5754) exploiting speculative execution to read kernel memory from user space before the permission check completes. Mitigated by KPTI (kernel page-table isolation).
Compiler-emitted code pattern (-mretpoline) replacing indirect jumps with a return-based sequence to prevent Spectre variant 2 branch target injection via the indirect branch predictor.

Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=address) injecting shadow-memory checks around every load/store to detect heap and stack buffer overflows, use-after-free, and double-free at ~2× runtime overhead.
Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=undefined) detecting undefined behavior at runtime: signed integer overflow, null pointer dereference, misaligned access. ~1.2× overhead. Use with ASan in CI.
Compiler instrumentation (-fsanitize=memory) detecting reads from uninitialized memory. ~3× overhead. Only works with Clang; requires all dependencies recompiled with MSan.
Compiler optimization removing writes to memory that are never subsequently read. Can silently remove memset() calls zeroing cryptographic secrets before free(), leaving key material in freed memory.

Coverage-guided fuzzer that mutates inputs and measures branch coverage to efficiently explore code paths. Pairs with ASan to detect memory safety bugs. Standard tool for finding crashes in C/C++ targets.
Utility inspecting an ELF binary for present security mitigations: NX, stack canary, PIE, RELRO, FORTIFY. First step in binary analysis to understand the exploit difficulty.

Tool reconstructing assembly from machine code (objdump, Ghidra, IDA Pro). Inherently lossy — no variable names, types, or intent. Variable-length x86 instructions make correct disassembly non-trivial.

Hardware-isolated secure processor (Apple Secure Enclave, Android StrongBox) for cryptographic operations and biometric verification. Code and data inside are inaccessible to the main OS even with root.
Apple's dedicated security chip in iPhone and Mac devices. Stores biometric templates and private keys for Touch/Face ID. Cryptographic operations happen inside; keys never leave it in plaintext.

Dynamic instrumentation framework for attaching to running processes on Android, iOS, and desktop. Injects a JavaScript engine to hook functions, bypass checks, and dump memory at runtime without modifying the binary.

Android bytecode format executed by the ART runtime. Compiled from Java/Kotlin source. Decompilable back to near-source-quality Java using Jadx — unlike native binaries, DEX retains significant structure.
Human-readable textual representation of Dalvik bytecode, analogous to assembly for the Android VM. Used to patch APK internals (disable checks, change logic) by editing Smali and repackaging.

Android's primary IPC mechanism for communication between components (Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver). Implicit intents are matched by OS to any exported component that declares a matching IntentFilter — a common attack surface.

An Android component (Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider) accessible from other apps because android:exported='true' is set or an IntentFilter is declared. Any app can send Intents to exported components.

Android wrapper that grants another component the right to fire a specific Intent with the creating app's identity. FLAG_MUTABLE allows the receiver to modify the Intent, enabling privilege escalation.
Open-source decompiler reconstructing Java/Kotlin source from Android DEX bytecode. Produces readable output suitable for finding hardcoded credentials, insecure logic, and obfuscation gaps.

Android's modern VM replacing Dalvik (Android 5+). Uses ahead-of-time compilation for performance. From a security perspective, DEX bytecode is still recoverable because ART metadata survives in the APK.

ZIP archive containing a compiled iOS app as a Mach-O binary plus resources. Downloaded from the App Store with FairPlay DRM encryption; decrypted by the device on install. Frida can dump the decrypted binary at runtime.

Lockheed Martin's seven-stage model of targeted attacks: Reconnaissance → Weaponization → Delivery → Exploitation → Installation → Command & Control → Actions on Objectives. Defenders break the chain at the earliest possible stage.

Nation-state or state-sponsored attacker with significant resources, proprietary zero-days, and long time horizons. Goals are intelligence collection, sabotage, or financial gain — not noisy opportunism.

Attacker-controlled infrastructure that communicates with compromised hosts after exploitation: receiving commands (execute, pivot, exfiltrate) and returning results. Often runs over HTTPS on port 443 to blend with normal traffic.
Post-exploitation technique of accessing additional systems within a network after an initial foothold, using stolen credentials, pass-the-hash, or exploitation of internal services.

Post-exploitation technique gaining higher access than initially obtained. Local: kernel exploits, misconfigured sudo, SUID binaries. Domain: Kerberoasting, DCSync. Goal is typically SYSTEM/root or Domain Admin.

Mass social engineering via email impersonating legitimate entities (banks, IT, SaaS vendors) to harvest credentials or deliver malware. Volume-based with low personalization. Effective because it targets humans, not systems.
Targeted phishing using personal information about the victim (name, role, colleagues, recent events). Significantly higher success rate than mass phishing. Common initial access technique for APTs.
Manipulation of people rather than systems to gain unauthorized access or information. Includes phishing, pretexting, vishing (voice), baiting (USB drops), and watering hole attacks.
Windows authentication attack using a captured NTLM hash directly without knowing the cleartext password. The hash is functionally equivalent to the password for NTLM authentication.

Active Directory attack requesting Kerberos service tickets for accounts with SPNs, then cracking them offline. Service accounts often have weak passwords and high privileges — a common privilege escalation path.

Security software monitoring endpoint processes, memory, and network behavior for attacker-indicative patterns. Evolved from signature-based AV. Detects post-exploitation (credential dumping, lateral movement) rather than just malware delivery.

Active Directory attack path visualization tool that maps group memberships, ACLs, and trust relationships to find shortest privilege escalation paths to Domain Admin. Used by both attackers and defenders.
Compromising a website frequented by the target organization to deliver malware to visitors. The attacker targets the website's visitors indirectly rather than the organization directly.

First stage of an attack: gathering information about the target via passive OSINT (LinkedIn, Shodan, DNS records) or active scanning (port scans, banner grabbing) to identify vulnerabilities and entry points.

XSS variant where the payload persists in the database and executes for every user who views the affected page — a multiplier attack. Higher impact than reflected XSS because it requires no victim interaction beyond visiting the page.

XSS variant where the payload is included in the request URL or body and reflected back in the response without storage. Requires tricking a victim into clicking a malicious link. Easier to find, harder to exploit at scale than stored XSS.

XSS variant entirely in client-side JavaScript: attacker-controlled data (location.hash, postMessage) flows to a dangerous DOM sink (innerHTML, eval, document.write) without server involvement. Not visible in server-side source code.

Vulnerability where a URL parameter controls the redirect destination without validation, allowing attackers to redirect victims to malicious sites using the trusted domain as a hop. Common in OAuth flows and phishing.

JavaScript vulnerability where attacker-controlled keys like __proto__ or constructor.prototype modify the prototype of all objects, injecting malicious properties that affect unrelated code paths across the application.

CSRF defense that sets a random value both as a cookie and as a hidden form field. The server validates both match. Attackers cannot read the cookie (SOP) so they cannot replicate it in the form field.

SSRF where the server makes the request but the response is not returned to the attacker. Exploited via out-of-band channels (DNS exfiltration, timing) to confirm the request occurred and infer information.

SQL injection where the payload is stored harmlessly but executes in a different code path when the stored data is later retrieved and used in a query without sanitization. Harder to find because the injection point and sink are separate.
SQL injection technique using UNION SELECT to append attacker-chosen query results alongside the application's legitimate results, extracting data from other tables directly in the response.

Database abstraction layer (Hibernate, Sequelize, SQLAlchemy, ActiveRecord) that typically generates parameterized queries and prevents SQLi. Raw query escape hatches (raw(), query()) bypass the protection and reintroduce injection risk.

JWT attack where the attacker changes the alg header field to exploit servers that trust the algorithm specified by the token (e.g., switching from RS256 to HS256, using the public key as the HMAC secret).
JWT algorithm value that disables signature verification. Some libraries accepted it without explicit configuration to reject it. A token with alg=none and any payload would be accepted as valid.

An access token passed in the Authorization HTTP header as "Bearer <token>". Whoever possesses the token is authenticated — there is no client proof of identity. Token theft grants full impersonation.

MFA second factor generating a 6-digit code from a shared secret and the current Unix timestamp (RFC 6238). Valid for ~30 seconds. Used in authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Authy). Susceptible to real-time phishing.

Built-in GraphQL query (__schema, __type) revealing the full schema: all types, fields, queries, and mutations. Useful for development but should be disabled in production to avoid exposing attack surface.

Issuing a new session ID after login or privilege change to prevent session fixation attacks. The old session ID is invalidated; the attacker who planted it gets no access after the victim authenticates.
Information leakage revealing whether a specific username or email exists, via different error messages, response times, or status codes. Enables targeted credential stuffing and phishing.

OAuth 2.0 flow for machine-to-machine authentication with no user involved. The client authenticates with its own client ID and secret to get an access token. Appropriate for backend services and daemons.

Hash-based Message Authentication Code. A keyed hash providing both integrity and authenticity: only someone with the key can produce a valid MAC. HMAC-SHA256 is the standard choice. Used in JWT (HS256), API request signing, and cookie verification.

Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. Produces compact signatures using elliptic curve math. Critical security requirement: the nonce (k) must be unique per signature — reusing a nonce leaks the private key (exploited against Sony PS3).

Safe RSA encryption using Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding. The randomized padding prevents deterministic ciphertext and is resistant to chosen-ciphertext attacks. Textbook RSA (no padding) is insecure.
TLS property where ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) generates a new session key per connection. Compromise of the server's long-term private key does not decrypt past recorded sessions.
Modern AEAD cipher standardized in TLS 1.3. Faster than AES-GCM on platforms without hardware AES acceleration (mobile, IoT). Provides confidentiality (ChaCha20) and authentication (Poly1305).

Function transforming a password or key material into a cryptographic key. Password KDFs (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2) add cost to resist brute force. Key KDFs (HKDF) expand/extract keys from shared secrets.

The integrity check output of AEAD encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), typically 128 bits. Validates that the ciphertext has not been tampered with. Must be verified before decryption; failure means reject.

Raw RSA encryption without padding: ciphertext = plaintext^e mod n. Deterministic, malleable, and vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext attacks. Never use in practice — always use RSA-OAEP for encryption or RSA-PSS for signatures.

Linux kernel mechanism (Secure Computing Mode) restricting which syscalls a process can make via a BPF filter. Default Docker seccomp profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls. A key layer in container security after namespace isolation.

Linux Security Module providing per-application mandatory access control via profiles defining allowed files, capabilities, and network access. Docker uses AppArmor profiles to restrict container filesystem access.

Kernel feature providing isolated views of system resources (pid, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user) for containerized processes. Each container has its own namespace; processes inside cannot see resources outside.

Linux kernel feature enforcing resource limits (CPU, memory, I/O, processes) on groups of processes. Prevents a container from consuming all host resources (DoS). Also provides accounting and resource isolation.

Fine-grained breakdown of root privileges into ~40 individual capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, etc.). Containers should drop all capabilities and add only those needed, rather than running as root.

Container image containing only the application binary and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no standard utilities. Dramatically reduces attack surface by removing tools an attacker would use post-exploitation.

Open-source multi-purpose vulnerability scanner from Aqua Security. Scans container images, filesystems, Git repos, and IaC (Terraform, Kubernetes) for CVEs and misconfigurations. Standard CI tool for container security.

Short-lived credentials generated on demand by a secrets manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) and automatically revoked after a TTL or checkout. Eliminates long-lived static credentials; breach impact is bounded to the TTL.

AWS Organizations policy setting maximum permission guardrails across member accounts. Even if an IAM policy in a member account grants full S3 access, an SCP denying S3 takes precedence organization-wide.

CNCF runtime security tool that monitors Linux kernel syscalls and container activity for anomalous behavior (shell in container, unexpected network connections, privilege escalation). Complements static scanning.

AWS managed threat detection service that analyzes CloudTrail API logs, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs to identify suspicious activity (cryptocurrency mining, data exfiltration, credential abuse) without agents.

Tool from the Sigstore project for signing and verifying container images. Supports keyless signing using an OIDC provider identity (GitHub Actions, Google) tied to a short-lived certificate in the Rekor transparency log.

Linux Foundation project providing free, transparent code signing infrastructure. Components: Cosign (signing tool), Rekor (append-only transparency log), Fulcio (CA issuing short-lived certs from OIDC identity).

Kubernetes built-in admission control levels applied per-namespace: Privileged (no restrictions), Baseline (blocks known privilege escalation), Restricted (hardened, no root, no host namespaces). Replaces deprecated PodSecurityPolicy.

A dependency of a dependency, not directly declared by your project. The majority of software supply chain vulnerabilities (Log4Shell, XZ utils) affect transitive, not direct, dependencies — often invisible without an SBOM.

Build practice ensuring identical source plus identical build environment always produces bit-for-bit identical output. Allows independent third parties to verify that a published binary matches its claimed source code.

Build that cannot access the internet or external state during execution; all dependencies are pre-fetched and specified as declared inputs. Prevents dependency substitution attacks and ensures builds are fully auditable.

ISO/IEC 5962 standard format for Software Bills of Materials. Expresses packages, versions, licenses, and relationships. Supported by most SBOM tooling; widely used for license compliance in addition to security.

OWASP SBOM format optimized for security use cases. Supports vulnerability metadata, service dependencies, and formulation (build process). More security-focused than SPDX; native format for Grype and Trivy output.

Free, machine-readable vulnerability database from Google covering npm, PyPI, Maven, Go, Rust, and more. Powers many SCA tools. Provides precise affected version ranges and fix versions in a normalized schema.

Secret scanner that analyzes git history including deleted commits to find leaked credentials. Detects secrets using regex and entropy analysis across all branches and all history — not just the current HEAD.

Fast open-source secret detection tool with configurable TOML rules. Run as a pre-commit hook or in CI to prevent secrets from entering version control. Reports file, line, and rule match for each finding.
Rate limiting algorithm processing requests at a fixed output rate from a queue. Bursts are buffered; excess beyond queue capacity is dropped. Smooths traffic but adds latency during bursts.

Rate limiting algorithm tracking request count over the last N seconds continuously. Prevents boundary burst attacks that fixed-window counters allow (all requests at the end of one window and start of the next).

HTTP response header controlling browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation, payment) available to the page and its embedded iframes. Successor to Feature-Policy. Limits damage from XSS and malicious third-party scripts.

Security testing technique injecting instrumentation into the running application to track taint flow from sources to sinks in real time. More accurate than DAST (sees internal state), no false positives on unreachable paths.
Open-source vulnerability scanner from Anchore for container images and filesystems. Outputs CVE matches against the installed package list. Integrates with CycloneDX and SPDX SBOM formats.
Linux utility tracing all syscalls made by a process and its children. Useful for dynamic analysis: reveals file opens, network connections, and exec calls without source code or symbols.
